column5: Creation of vegetation
column6: The commentary’s third “who” names the Lord by bringing forth pasture; Genesis has God command the earth to sprout seed-bearing vegetation, placing plant emergence within the creation scene.

column5: Green plants as animal food
column6: The commentary reads merʿā as pasture seen by the mouths that eat it; Genesis assigns green plants to the beasts, making the pasture’s animal sustenance explicit.

column5: Hebrew רעה, tending a flock
column6: The commentary records Arabic merʿā under r-ʿ-y; Genesis uses the likely cognate Hebrew root רעה for Joseph tending the flock, showing the pastoral action in its own narrative rather than treating the Arabic noun as a dictionary gloss.

column5: Pasture and household livelihood
column6: The commentary places green pasture outside the tent and among the foundations of pastoral life; Jacob’s sons explain that they have come to settle where pasture is available for their flocks, showing its material role in a herding household.

column5: Grass for livestock and human fullness
column6: The commentary says pasture feeds the herd that sustains people; Moses promises grass in the fields for livestock and food until the people are full, joining the two beneficiaries.

column5: Rain where no human lives
column6: The commentary notes that 87:4 names neither rain nor soil and shifts attention to the one who brings out grass; Job describes God sending rain on land without people, supplying the omitted weather source while stressing divine agency beyond human cultivation.

column5: Grass brought forth in wilderness
column6: The commentary treats pasture as something the Lord brings out of hidden ground; Job says the rain makes grass sprout in desolate places, a direct picture of vegetation appearing by divine provision.

column5: Hebrew רעה, the Lord as shepherd
column6: The commentary notes that merʿā belongs to the r-ʿ-y family also used for a shepherd’s work; Psalm 23 predicates that Hebrew cognate of the Lord, making explicit the pastoral sense that the Qur’anic wording leaves implicit.

column5: Green pasture and rest
column6: The commentary says merʿā unites grass, grazing place, and the act of grazing; the psalm’s shepherd makes the speaker lie down in green pastures and leads him beside water, bringing those linked images together.

column5: Watering furrows and blessing growth
column6: The commentary reads pasture as the land’s recurring yield under the Lord’s measure; the psalm describes God watering furrows and softening earth so its growth is blessed, joining measured water to yield.

column5: Pastures, flocks, and grain at year’s end
column6: The commentary calls pasture the land’s annual yield for herds; the psalm pictures pastures clothed with flocks and valleys covered with grain, then making joyful sounds, a close pastoral harvest scene.

column5: Grass for cattle, plants for people
column6: The commentary says the word merʿā views vegetation as food for the creature that grazes; the psalm says God makes grass grow for cattle and plants for human work, naming the same giver and both uses.

column5: Every creature waits for food in season
column6: The commentary treats pasture as one creature’s provision from the Lord; the psalm says all creatures wait for God to give food at its proper time, expanding the individual pasture into universal dependence.

column5: Renewing the face of the ground
column6: The commentary follows green growth into decay and sees the Lord as the source of emergence; the psalm says God sends forth spirit and renews the ground, giving the vegetation cycle a creation-and-renewal frame.

column5: Praise in response to creation
column6: The commentary begins with a command to glorify the Lord and identifies him through creation and pasture; the psalmist vows to sing to the Lord while alive, placing praise directly in response to the created order.

column5: Clouds, rain, and grass on hills
column6: The commentary hears the unmentioned rain behind the pasture that God brings forth; the psalm explicitly connects God’s cloud-cover and rain with grass growing on the mountains.

column5: Food for beasts from the same giver
column6: The commentary says pasture names vegetation as the herd’s food; the psalm says God gives food to animals and young ravens, extending the provision claim beyond the flock.

column5: Teaching descending like rain and dew
column6: The commentary links the grass passage to the later recitation and instruction; Moses asks that his teaching fall like rain and his speech distill like dew, joining divine teaching to the water that makes growth possible.

column5: Rain yields seed and bread
column6: The commentary reads pasture as growth produced by water and later contrasts it with the recited word; Isaiah says rain and snow water earth, making it yield seed for sowing and bread for eating, a precise provision chain.

column5: The spoken word accomplishes its purpose
column6: The commentary connects the Lord who brings out pasture with the word later recited and retained; Isaiah’s next verse says the word from God’s mouth does not return empty but accomplishes its purpose, explicitly setting word beside the rain-and-seed image.

column5: Grass fades while God’s word stands
column6: The commentary contrasts the pasture that becomes dark debris with the recitation that remains; Isaiah says grass withers but God’s word stands forever, giving the same concrete contrast between perishable vegetation and enduring speech.

column5: The earth gives birth to the dead
column6: The commentary treats recurring growth from dead ground as a sign that the dead can be brought out; Isaiah calls the earth to give birth to its dead, making the earth’s production image explicitly serve resurrection hope.

column5: A heavenly command over each blade of grass
column6: The commentary presents each emergence of pasture as a gift whose hidden growth belongs to God; this midrash says no blade of grass lacks a heavenly constellation that strikes it and commands it to grow, interpreting ordinary growth as supervised providence.

column5: Seed grows while the sower does not know how
column6: The commentary describes growth from an unseen seed and root as an act whose source is the Lord; Jesus’ parable says the seed sprouts and grows while the person who scattered it does not know how, making hidden growth the point of the image.

column5: Earth yields successive stages
column6: The commentary follows pasture from concealed seed to visible green; the parable says the earth produces first a blade, then an ear, then full grain, a direct sequence of emergence and maturation.

column5: Growth reaches harvest
column6: The commentary calls pasture the land’s yield and follows it to its later end; Jesus’ parable ends when the grain is ripe and the sickle is put in, tying emergence to the harvest that follows.

column5: God gives the growth
column6: The commentary insists that the Lord, rather than the human observer, is the one who brings pasture out; Paul says neither planter nor waterer counts, but God who gives the growth, an explicit account of divine agency in cultivation.

column5: A seed dies before it comes to life
column6: The commentary reads pasture’s greening and subsequent decay as an analogy that makes resurrection imaginable; Paul says what is sown does not come to life unless it dies, using the plant cycle as his argument for resurrection.

column5: Perishable sowing and imperishable raising
column6: The commentary contrasts grass that ends as debris with the human future that is raised into what lasts; Paul explicitly contrasts what is sown perishable with what is raised imperishable.

column5: All flesh is like grass
column6: The commentary follows pasture from green growth to its end; Peter quotes Isaiah that all flesh is grass and its glory like a flower, applying vegetation’s short life to human life.

column5: The Lord’s word endures as gospel proclamation
column6: The commentary contrasts the grass that withers with the recitation that remains; Peter says the Lord’s word endures and identifies it with the good news preached to the readers, making the word/grass contrast an apostolic proclamation claim.

column5: Creation grounds praise
column6: The commentary’s praise call is followed by claims about the Lord creating and sustaining pasture; Revelation’s elders praise the Lord as worthy because he created all things, a compact Christian doxology grounded in creation.

column5: Created food calls for thanksgiving
column6: The commentary joins the Lord’s creative provision of pasture to glorification; the Didache’s meal thanksgiving says the Almighty created all things and gave food and drink so people might thank him, making the provision-to-praise relation liturgical.

column5: Field growth before rain or cultivation
column6: The commentary emphasizes that 87:4 leaves soil and rain unnamed and foregrounds the one who brings pasture out; Genesis describes the field before rain and before a human works the ground, clarifying the conditions whose absence the short Qur’anic clause leaves unstated.

column5: God makes trees grow from the ground
column6: The commentary describes grass rising from hidden seed and soil; Genesis says God makes trees grow from the ground, a related but broader account of vegetation’s emergence.

column5: Moses leads a flock to Horeb
column6: The commentary recalls Moses’ years as a shepherd and links that work to his later encounter at the fire; Exodus places Moses at Horeb while leading his father-in-law’s flock, grounding the shepherd-to-revelation sequence in another scripture.

column5: Theophany while Moses is tending sheep
column6: The commentary moves from Moses’ staff for tending sheep to the fire where revelation begins; Exodus has the bush blaze before Moses in the same scene, preserving the concrete meeting of pastoral work and divine appearance.

column5: Abraham trusts God to provide
column6: The commentary presents Abraham’s Lord as the one who feeds and sustains him; at the binding of Isaac, Abraham tells his son that God will provide the offering, giving divine provision a specific Abrahamic scene.

column5: Abraham receives Isaac back from death
column6: The commentary’s Abrahamic sequence names the Lord as the one who kills and gives life; Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise Isaac and so received him back figuratively from death, interpreting the binding story through resurrection.

column5: Blessing after eating one is full
column6: The commentary presents grass and food as a free gift that ends in glorifying the giver; Moses commands Israel to bless the Lord after eating and becoming full, making gratitude the human response to provision.

column5: Harvest left for the poor and sojourner
column6: The commentary says a yield received without payment still carries a duty to give others their share; Leviticus forbids harvesting a field to its edge and leaves gleanings for the poor and the sojourner, specifying the social obligation attached to produce.

column5: A forgotten sheaf belongs to the vulnerable
column6: The commentary connects free yield with giving a due from the harvest; Deuteronomy leaves a forgotten sheaf for the sojourner, orphan, and widow, turning that connection into a concrete harvest law.

column5: A cut tree can sprout again
column6: The commentary takes recurring green growth as evidence that life can emerge after apparent death; Job says a felled tree can sprout again when it smells water, then contrasts that hope with human mortality, making the plant-to-human analogy vivid but unsettled.

column5: Job leaves human resurrection as a question
column6: The commentary uses grass renewed from the earth to make the dead’s return plausible; after describing a tree’s regrowth, Job asks whether a dead human can live again, so the same natural analogy ends in an open question rather than an asserted answer.

column5: A fruitful tree beside water
column6: The commentary says growth follows from water and that the visible green is a gift; the righteous person in the psalm is like a tree planted by streams that yields fruit in season, giving water-fed vegetation an ethical image.

column5: Chaff blown away
column6: The commentary’s pasture becomes dark debris and illustrates the passing life of this world; the psalm calls the wicked chaff driven by wind, using light plant remains for a moral image rather than a botanical cycle.

column5: Grass that flourishes and withers in a day
column6: The commentary follows the pasture’s green life into decay; the psalm compares human life to grass that flourishes in the morning and withers by evening, applying the same daily plant arc to mortality.

column5: Human days like grass
column6: The commentary sets pasture’s brief green phase against what lasts beyond this life; the psalm says a human’s days are like grass and flourish like a field flower, making the plant’s brevity a figure for human transience.

column5: Wind erases the flower’s place
column6: The commentary says the plant is turned into debris and disappears; the psalm says wind passes over the field flower and it is gone so its place knows it no more, sharpening the disappearance image.

column5: Mercy outlasts human life
column6: The commentary turns from pasture’s short life to the Hereafter as better and more enduring; the psalm contrasts grass-like human days with the Lord’s everlasting steadfast love, supplying a close theological contrast of mortal vegetation and lasting divine good.

column5: Attend carefully to the flock
column6: The commentary gives the shepherd’s work a sense of watching over the herd and its future; Proverbs tells the keeper to know the state of his flock and attend to the herds, making that practical oversight explicit in its own pastoral setting.

column5: The divine shepherd settles the flock in good pasture
column6: The commentary says the Qur’anic clause names the one who brings pasture but does not call God a shepherd; Ezekiel explicitly depicts God feeding his flock and settling it in good pasture, showing how another scripture makes the shepherd-pasture connection explicit.

column5: God’s word runs through the earth
column6: The commentary juxtaposes the Lord’s pasture-making with the Prophet’s recitation; elsewhere in the same psalm God sends his command through the earth before the cloud, grass, and animal-food lines, placing word and created provision within one hymn.

column5: A green tree endures drought by water
column6: The commentary’s plant grows and then withers, while its creator sustains life; Jeremiah pictures a tree planted by water whose leaf stays green and which does not cease bearing fruit in drought, a counter-image of sustained rather than seasonal growth.

column5: Blessing acknowledges the world’s owner
column6: The commentary says the Lord provides pasture without demanding a fee; the rabbis teach that one may not enjoy the world before blessing God, because the earth belongs to God, adding human acknowledgment to apparently free provision.

column5: A blessing for produce of the ground
column6: The commentary begins with glorification and then names vegetation as the Lord’s provision; the Mishnah assigns a blessing to fruit of the ground, showing how ordinary produce becomes a spoken act of praise.

column5: Field grass is temporary yet clothed by God
column6: The commentary describes pasture becoming dark debris and treats vegetation as provision from its maker; Jesus says grass is in the field today and thrown into the oven tomorrow, yet God clothes it, joining transience to divine care.

column5: Pasture through the gate
column6: The commentary notes that merʿā carries pasture and grazing while the root also names a shepherd’s work; Jesus says those entering through him will be saved and find pasture, placing the pasture image in a Christian shepherd-and-access teaching.

column5: Human planting and watering depend on God
column6: The commentary emphasizes that the Lord, not the human observer, brings pasture out; Paul describes himself planting and Apollos watering before saying God caused growth, distinguishing human labor from the source of life.

column5: The rich person fades like a field flower
column6: The commentary uses the plant’s short life to frame the contrast between this world and what endures; James says the rich person passes away like grass and its flower, applying the same fading image to worldly status.
